title: Somebody Has to Hold It Up
part: PART FOUR: HOLDING UP THE BRIDGE

pages.text:
*From the Bridgewater Almanac: A good bridge is a bridge that has never had to be thought about.*

The rain came down in a grey curtain, turning the Founders’ Green into a soup of mud and leaves. The town crossed the old bridge from both sides, a brass band playing out of tune and two hundred umbrellas blooming in the mist. The Mayor led the way, his top hat shining, beaming as if he had invented the parade himself.

At the back, Rue, Perrin, and Skye held a sign that said nothing. A stone had smudged the ink during the night, leaving only a vague, gray smear. It looked less like a warning and more like a stain of tea. Rue kept glancing at the bridge. The stones looked the same as always, wet and dark, but the air felt thin.

"Let them pass," Skye whispered, her braid damp and heavy. "We can't stop a parade."

Rue wanted to argue. She wanted to say that the bridge was not a parade. It was a structure. But the brass band played a loud, brassy note, and the first row of umbrellas reached the middle stone.
pages.image: A rainy market square with a long line of people in coats and umbrellas crossing a stone arch bridge; a brass band plays at the front while a small freckled girl and two other children hold a blank, smudged paper sign at the rear, looking anxious.

pages.text:
The middle stone groaned. It was not a crack, not yet, but a deep, resonant hum that vibrated through the soles of everyone’s boots. The sound was like a great animal turning over in its sleep, slow and heavy and full of pain.

A crack raced up the parapet, white against the gray stone, and the bridge sagged. It dropped a hand's breadth, just enough to make the umbrellas tilt and the rain splash into people’s faces. The brass band stopped. The Mayor stopped mid-speech, his mouth open, his top hat suddenly looking very small and very fragile.

Cedric was in the middle of the bridge. He stood with his hands at his sides, his red waistcoat bright against the dull stone. He did not look afraid. He looked frozen. The crack widened, and a piece of gravel the size of a pea fell into the river below with a tiny, insignificant splash.
pages.image: A close-up of a stone bridge arch cracking in the center; a skinny boy in a red waistcoat stands frozen on the wet stones, surrounded by people holding tilted umbrellas, while a piece of gravel falls toward the dark river below.

pages.text:
Then the water moved. It did not splash or roar; it simply parted, pulling back from the stone the way a shy child steps away from a loud room. From beneath the arch, a hand the size of a dinner table rose out of the River Wend. It was grey-green and mossy, with thick fingers and a palm marked by deep, weathered lines.

The hand laid itself flat against the broken span, holding it steady. Behind it, a shoulder emerged, broad enough to block out the rain. The back was covered in patches of green moss and lichen, damp and heavy. Finally, a head rose, streaming with water. It was Hobb. He wore his patched waistcoat, and his round spectacles hung by a single piece of twine, drooping over one eye. He was not looking at the town. He was looking at the stone, his brow furrowed in deep concentration, his small tusks visible above his lower lip.
pages.image: A giant mossy troll emerging from the river to hold up a bridge arch; his large hand presses against the stone, his face is kind but strained, rain streams from his hair, and his spectacles are mended with twine.

pages.text:
Hobb’s voice came from deep inside his chest, steady and clear. It cut right through the sound of the water and the hush of the crowd.

"Walk," he said. "Please. I have you. Walk slowly and don't look down."

No one moved. The rain dripped from the brims of their hats. Rue felt her stomach do a strange, tight flip, like she had just swallowed a whole lemon pectin. She looked at Perrin, who was staring at the troll with wide eyes. She looked at Skye, whose hand was trembling.

"Right then," Rue said.

The words came out small, but they were firm. She stepped out onto the bridge, her rubber boots squelching on the wet stone. She walked to the middle, where Cedric stood. She reached out and took his hand. He let her. His fingers were cold, but they were still.

Perrin took Skye’s hand. One by one, they began to cross.
pages.image: A small freckled girl in a yellow raincoat holding the hand of a skinny boy in a red waistcoat on a wet stone bridge; behind them, a tall girl and a boy in a wool hat follow, while a giant mossy troll supports the bridge from below.

pages.text:
It took eleven minutes. They were the longest eleven minutes of Rue’s life. She counted every step, every crack in the stone, every drop of rain that hit the water. The bridge groaned, but it held. Hobb held it.

The Mayor was the last to cross. He clutched his top hat in both hands, his face pale, and walked slowly, carefully, under Hobb’s bowed head. He did not look at the troll. He did not look at the bridge. He simply moved, step by step, until he was safe on the far bank.

When the last person was across, Hobb’s knees began to shake. The great mossy legs trembled, and the bridge shuddered. He exhaled, a long, weary sound that smelled of river water and old paper.

"Somebody," he said, through his teeth, his voice rough and tired, "has to hold it up."
pages.image: A giant mossy troll kneeling in the river, supporting the bridge with his shoulders, his expression tired and strained; a round man in a top hat stands on the far bank, looking down with a solemn expression, rain falling around them.
